/-!
# Mahler's Z-numbers

A *Z-number* is a positive real number `ξ` such that the fractional part of
`ξ (3/2)^n` lies in `[0, 1/2)` for every positive integer `n`. Mahler asked
whether any Z-number exists; this is still open.

*References*:
- [Mah68] Mahler, Kurt. "An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2."
  Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society 8.2 (1968): 313-321.
- [Wikipedia, Mahler's 3/2 problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem)

## Main definitions

* `IsZNumber`: a real number is a Z-number.
-/

/-- A **Z-number** is a positive real number `ξ` such that the fractional part of
`ξ (3/2)^n` lies in `[0, 1/2)` for every positive integer `n`. -/
def IsZNumber (ξ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  0 < ξ ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → Int.fract (ξ * (3 / 2 : ℝ) ^ n) < 1 / 2

findings.description: The reusable predicate adopts Wikipedia's n ≥ 1 convention, but Mahler's original definition and Bugeaud's definition include n = 0. Thus the Lean predicate does not require Int.fract ξ < 1/2. The precise relationship is IsZNumber ξ ↔ Z₀ (ξ * (3/2)), where Z₀ uses every natural index; this is not an equivalence at the same argument. The convention is explicitly documented and follows one cited source, so this is a modelling question rather than a definite misformalization. All current nonexistence, measure-zero, and Hausdorff-dimension uses are invariant under this dilation.
findings.source_evidence: Mahler (1968), p. 313, definition (1), requires the inequalities for all n ≥ 0: https://doi.org/10.1017/S1446788700005371. Bugeaud (2012), §3.2, p. 50, likewise defines a positive real Z-number using all integers n ≥ 0 (Google Books excerpt). In contrast, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem explicitly says 'all positive integers n'.
findings.suggested_fix: Prefer the primary-literature convention: `0 < ξ ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, Int.fract (ξ * (3 / 2 : ℝ) ^ n) < 1 / 2`, updating the docstrings to 'nonnegative integers'. Alternatively, explicitly distinguish the two conventions and provide the dilation equivalence, rather than presenting the positive-index convention without noting its difference from [Mah68].

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/Mahler32.lean, lines 42–45, the implication is reversed. Lean assumes that no Z-number exists and concludes Ω(3/2) > 1/2. The cited source gives Ω(3/2) > 1/2 as a sufficient condition for nonexistence, not as a consequence. A Z-number supplies an orbit of limiting width at most 1/2, proving the source's direction. I proved that direction independently in /workspace/review/consequence.lean without using the problem files' sorry proofs. The converse is an additional assertion, not established by this argument or the cited source.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia states: 'Mahler's conjecture would follow if Ω(3/2) exceeds 1/2.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem
findings.suggested_fix: Reverse the hypothesis and conclusion: `theorem mahler_conjecture.variants.consequence (hΩ : 1 / 2 < Ω (3 / 2)) : type_of% mahler_conjecture := ...`. Update the docstring accordingly.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/Mahler32.lean, lines 48–51, the result attributed to Flatto–Lagarias–Pollington has a strict bound `1 / p < Ω (p / q)`. Their theorem states the non-strict bound `1 / p ≤ Ω (p / q)`. The strict sign also appears on Wikipedia, but disagrees with the primary paper cited there. Excluding equality is an additional mathematical assertion; it does not follow from the paper's lower bound or from taking an infimum.
findings.source_evidence: Flatto, Lagarias and Pollington, 'On the range of fractional parts {ξ(p/q)^n}', Acta Arithmetica 70 (1995), Theorem 1.4, p. 129, states limsup − liminf ≥ 1/p for every positive ξ. Page 130 explicitly restates this as Ω(p/q) ≥ 1/p. https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-70-2-125-147; full paper read at https://www.impan.pl/shop/publication/transaction/download/product/108521. Wikipedia instead prints a strict inequality.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `<` with `≤` in the theorem and `>` with `≥` in its docstring, and cite Theorem 1.4 directly. Retain a strict strengthening only with a separate source establishing it.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/Books/BugeaudDistributionModuloOne/Problem10_9.lean, lines 36–41, the docstring says there are 'no real numbers ξ' satisfying the displayed inequalities. Literally, ξ = 0 satisfies them for every positive n. The Lean statement correctly excludes zero, since the imported IsZNumber includes `0 < ξ`. This is a documentation omission, not a defect in the Lean nonexistence statement.
findings.source_evidence: Mahler (1968), p. 313, begins with a positive number; Bugeaud §3.2, p. 50, and the cited Wikipedia definition also explicitly require positivity. The scratch checks prove both that zero satisfies every displayed fractional-part bound and that `¬ IsZNumber 0`.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to 'There are no positive real numbers ξ ...'.

reformulations.difference: Compared with Mahler's original n ≥ 0 definition, the nonexistence statement uses the library's n ≥ 1 predicate.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Writing Z₀ for the original definition, IsZNumber ξ ↔ Z₀ ((3/2)ξ). Hence existence, and therefore nonexistence, is equivalent under the two conventions. The nonexistence iff was proved explicitly in scratch.lean. This does not identify the two predicates at an unchanged argument.

reformulations.difference: The set in Lean uses positive indices, whereas the set treated in Mahler's paper includes index zero.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The Lean set is the inverse image of the original set under multiplication by 3/2, so its Lebesgue measure is 2/3 times the original measure. Multiplication by this positive finite constant preserves vanishing. The measure-zero iff was proved in scratch.lean using Real.volume_preimage_mul_right.

reformulations.difference: The Hausdorff-dimension claim uses the positive-index Z-number set rather than the original zero-index set.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Multiplication by 3/2 maps the Lean set bijectively onto the original set and is bi-Lipschitz. Their Hausdorff dimensions are therefore equal. Both the dimension equality and the resulting `< 1` iff were proved in scratch.lean.

review.notes: Apart from the indexing-convention question, IsZNumber matches its docstring and Wikipedia exactly. Int.fract automatically supplies the omitted nonnegative lower bound; both divisions are real; positivity excludes the trivial zero orbit; and the strict upper endpoint correctly rejects ξ = 1 at n = 1. No Mathlib duplicate was found. Mahler actually proves countability, which also supports the inspected measure-zero and dimension corollaries after dilation. The implication and strict-bound findings are additional errors in an inspected use-site file, not defects caused by Int.fract. All three scratch files in /workspace/review/ compiled successfully; the substantive independent proofs use only standard Lean axioms, not sorryAx. No reviewed repository file was modified.
